content: High-flow nasal cannulae (HFNC) deliver a combination of humidified air and oxygen at high flow rates through wide-bore nasal prongs. This method is used to provide respiratory support for adults in the intensive care unit (ICU) who are experiencing or at risk of acute respiratory failure. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of HFNC compared to standard oxygen therapy, non-invasive ventilation (NIV), or non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) in adults admitted to the ICU. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared HFNC with other non-invasive respiratory support methods, such as standard oxygen therapy (via nasal cannulae or mask) or NIV/NIPPV (including continuous positive airway pressure and bilevel positive airway pressure). A total of 31 studies involving 5136 participants were included in this review, with 20 new studies added since the previous version. Among these, 21 studies compared HFNC with standard oxygen therapy, and 13 studies compared HFNC with NIV or NIPPV. Three studies included both comparisons. Additionally, 51 ongoing studies (estimated 12,807 participants) and 19 studies awaiting classification were identified. In 18 studies, HFNC was initiated after extubation, while in the remaining studies, participants had not been previously mechanically ventilated. HFNC versus Standard Oxygen Therapy: HFNC may reduce treatment failure, as indicated by a lower likelihood of escalation to alternative oxygen therapies (risk ratio [RR] 0.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.45 to 0.86; low-certainty evidence). HFNC probably has little or no effect on mortality compared to standard oxygen therapy (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.11; moderate-certainty evidence). HFNC likely results in little or no difference in the incidence of pneumonia (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.09; moderate-certainty evidence). The effect of HFNC on nasal mucosa or skin trauma is uncertain (RR 3.66, 95% CI 0.43 to 31.48; very low-certainty evidence). HFNC may have little or no impact on ICU length of stay (mean difference [MD] 0.12 days, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.27; low-certainty evidence). The effect of HFNC on the ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen to the fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) within 24 hours of treatment is uncertain (MD 10.34 mmHg, 95% CI -17.31 to 38; very low-certainty evidence). HFNC’s impact on short-term comfort (MD 0.31, 95% CI -0.60 to 1.22; very low-certainty evidence) and long-term comfort (MD 0.59, 95% CI -2.29 to 3.47; very low-certainty evidence) is also uncertain. HFNC versus NIV or NIPPV: There was no evidence of a difference in treatment failure when HFNC was used post-extubation or without prior mechanical ventilation (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.22; low-certainty evidence). HFNC likely has little or no effect on in-hospital mortality compared to NIV or NIPPV (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.31; low-certainty evidence). The effect of HFNC on the incidence of pneumonia is very uncertain (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.17 to 1.52; very low-certainty evidence). HFNC may result in little or no difference in the risk of barotrauma (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.42 to 3.14; low-certainty evidence). HFNC may have little or no impact on ICU length of stay (MD -0.72 days, 95% CI -2.85 to 1.42; low-certainty evidence). The PaO2/FiO2 ratio may be lower up to 24 hours after HFNC use (MD -58.10 mmHg, 95% CI -71.68 to -44.51; low-certainty evidence). The effect of HFNC on short-term comfort, as measured by comfort scores (MD 1.33, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.92; very low-certainty evidence) and questionnaire responses (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.53; very low-certainty evidence), is uncertain. No studies reported on the impact of HFNC on nasal mucosa or skin trauma in this comparison. Conclusions: HFNC may reduce treatment failure compared to standard oxygen therapy, but it likely has little or no effect on treatment failure when compared to NIV or NIPPV. For most other outcomes, there was no evidence of a significant difference between HFNC and the other respiratory support methods. However, the certainty of the evidence was often low or very low. A large number of ongoing studies may provide more robust evidence in future updates and could potentially alter these findings.
